evidence.gloss: FAQ answering what CPH is, how to calculate it, and the average 2026 cost per hire by role level, restating the SHRM benchmarks and formula.
evidence.verbatim:
What is cost per hire?
Cost per hire (CPH) is the standardised talent acquisition metric measuring the total investment required to source, attract, assess, and onboard a new employee. The authoritative SHRM/ANSI formula is: CPH = (Total Internal Recruiting Costs + Total External Recruiting Costs) / Total Number of Hires. Per SHRM 2026 Talent Access Benchmarking Report, average US CPH is approximately $4,700-$4,800 for non-executive roles and $28,329-$35,879 for executive hires.
How do you calculate cost per hire?
Use the SHRM/ANSI formula: CPH = (Internal Costs + External Costs) / Total Hires. Internal costs include recruiter salaries and overhead, hiring manager and interviewer time, HR administrative time, recruiting technology (ATS, sourcing tools), internal referral bonuses, and recruiting events. External costs include job board postings, recruitment advertising, agency or retained search fees, background checks and assessments, sign-on bonuses, relocation, and candidate travel. Divide all recruiting costs in a period by all hires made in that same period.
What’s the average cost per hire in 2026?
Per SHRM 2026 Talent Access Benchmarking Report: approximately $4,700-$4,800 for non-executive roles (US average). Executive roles average $28,329-$35,879 (up 21% from 2022). Significant variation by role: entry-level $1,500-$3,500; mid-level professional $3,500-$8,000; engineering $6,000-$23,000; senior management $10,000-$30,000; retained executive search $50,000-$250,000. Technology and financial services above average; retail and hospitality below average.
What costs are missing from the SHRM cost per hire formula?
The SHRM/ANSI formula does not include vacancy cost (productivity loss while a role sits empty), which is often larger than the recruiting investment. Per industry research: standard professional roles lose ~$500/day; revenue-generating sales roles lose $7,000-$10,000/month. With median 2026 US time-to-fill at 63.5 days, vacancy cost typically adds $22,000+ to the SHRM CPH for standard roles. Also excluded: ramp cost (new hires below full productivity for 3-12 months) and quality risk.
How do you reduce cost per hire?
Invest in employee referrals (consistently lowest CPH and highest quality), build internal sourcing capability (reduce agency dependence), optimise candidate experience (lower drop-off improves yield), use AI tools (mature implementations cut CPH 30%+), reduce time-to-fill (compounds savings via vacancy cost), track source-of-hire ROI rigorously, audit agency relationships, and build talent pools (pre-engaged candidates reduce future CPH dramatically).
Is a lower cost per hire always better?
No. If low-CPH hires leave quickly or underperform, the true hiring cost is much higher. CPH should be tracked alongside quality-of-hire, time-to-fill, candidate experience, source-of-hire effectiveness, and 90-day / 1-year retention. Quality-adjusted CPH, the cost per successful, retained, and productive hire, is the metric that matters for business outcomes.

h3.h3: The formula behind the figure: external plus internal costs divided by total hires

evidence.gloss: Defines cost-per-hire as the total cost of hiring a new employee, including advertising, agency fees, referrals, and HR staff salaries.
evidence.verbatim: Cost-per-hire (CPH) is a key recruiting metric that tracks the total cost of hiring a new employee. This includes expenses such as advertising costs, recruitment agency fees, employee referrals, and the salaries of HR staff involved in the hiring process.

evidence.gloss: Explains the CPH formula (external + internal costs divided by total hires), defines external vs internal costs, and gives a worked $40,000/10-hires = $4,000 example.
evidence.verbatim:
The cost-per-hire calculator uses the following formula to calculate the total hiring costs:
Cost-per-hire (CPH)= (External costs) + (Internal costs) / Total number of hires in a period
External recruitment costs: These are expenses involved in hiring from outside sources (outside companies). Examples include salaries for recruitment agencies, advertising fees, recruitment technology, candidate travel costs, and pre-employment screening costs.
Internal recruitment costs: These are expenses involved in hiring from sources within a company. Examples include salaries for HR professionals or recruiting staff, operating internal job boards, rewards for employee referrals, interview costs, recruiter travel costs, etc.
Total number of employees hired: This involves the number of people recruited and onboarded, excluding whether they remained in the company afterward.
This metric is crucial for understanding the efficiency of hiring processes and helps organizations make informed budgeting decisions.
For instance, if a company spends $40,000 recruiting and hiring ten employees, the cost-per-hire would be $4,000. Monitoring CPH over time can also help identify trends and areas for improvement in the recruitment strategy.

evidence.gloss: Explains cost-per-hire calculation, cites the ~$4,700 SHRM average, and warns against optimizing for the cheapest hire.
evidence.verbatim: Cost-per-hire adds up advertising, agency fees, recruiter time, and tooling, then divides by the number of hires. SHRM benchmarking puts the average near $4,700, though it swings widely by role and seniority. Do not chase the lowest possible number. A cheap hire who leaves in six months is the most expensive kind, because Gallup estimates replacing someone costs one-half to two times their salary.

evidence.gloss: Breaks down Cost Per Hire into internal and external cost components, gives national average and role-level benchmarks, and starts unpacking the most important cost-per-hire insight.
evidence.verbatim:
Cost Per Hire is the total investment required to successfully fill one open position. It is a KPI that most organizations track in some form, but very few track honestly. The gap between what teams think they spend on hiring and what they actually spend is almost always significant.
Breaking down the true cost of hire
Internal costs include:
- Hiring manager and interview panel time (often overlooked but frequently the largest single cost component)
- HR technology and ATS licensing fees
- Employee referral bonuses
- Internal onboarding and training overhead
External costs include:
- Job board advertising fees (LinkedIn, Indeed, niche boards)
- Recruitment agency or executive search fees, which typically range from 15 to 25% of the first year’s salary
- Background screening and pre-employment assessment tools
- Employer branding and careers site investment
- Relocation packages and signing bonuses were applicable
What the benchmarks say
SHRM’s most recent data puts the average Cost Per Hire in the United States at approximately $4,700, but this figure masks enormous variation by role level and function. More realistic breakdowns look like this:
- Entry-level and high-volume roles: $1,500 to $3,000 per hire
- Mid-level professional roles: $5,000 to $10,000 per hire
- Senior individual contributors and managers: $15,000 to $30,000 per hire
- Director level and above with executive search involvement: $30,000 to $100,000 or more
The most important cost per hire insight
Cost per hire only becomes a genuinely useful metric when it is read alongside Quality of Hire. A $2,000 hire who exits in six months or underperforms for two years is dramatically more expensive than a $15,000 hire who stays for five years and exceeds expectations.
Teams that optimize cost per hire in isolation consistently make this mistake, cutting corners on sourcing, assessment, and candidate experience to reduce spend, and then wondering why retention and performance outcomes suffer.
The right question to ask is not “how do we lower cost per hire?” It is “how do we optimize cost per hire relative to the quality and longevity of the hires we make?”

What is the difference between direct and indirect hiring costs?
Direct hiring costs are the visible, measurable expenses tied to filling one role, such as job ads, agency fees, background checks, assessments, and a signing bonus. Indirect hiring costs are the harder-to-see expenses of the hiring effort itself: recruiter and interviewer time, lost team productivity, onboarding, and the cost of a wrong hire. Direct costs show up on an invoice. Indirect costs show up in your calendar and your output.
What are examples of indirect hiring costs?
Common indirect hiring costs include the hours your team spends screening resumes and interviewing, the dip in productivity while a role sits open or a new hire ramps, onboarding and training time, added admin work, lower morale on a stretched team, and the biggest one, a bad hire. Gallup puts the cost of replacing an employee at 50% to 200% of their annual salary.
Are salaries a direct or indirect cost?
Most salaries are treated as indirect costs because they support the business broadly rather than one specific product, project, or sale. The exception is when a person is hired for a single, traceable task, like a recruiter brought on only to fill one set of roles. That portion of pay is a direct cost because it maps to a specific activity.
What is the average cost to hire an employee in 2026?
SHRM benchmarking puts the average cost per hire at about $4,700, though it commonly ranges from $2,000 to more than $20,000 depending on the role, seniority, industry, and location. That figure usually reflects direct costs only. Add indirect costs like recruiter time and lost productivity and the real total often runs two to three times higher.
How can companies reduce direct and indirect hiring costs?
Tighten the process so fewer hours are wasted, build a warm talent pipeline, use internal mobility, and screen with structured skills assessments so the shortlist is scored before the first interview. Cutting mis-hires is the highest-impact move because a wrong hire is the most expensive indirect cost. Evidence-based screening is where most teams save the most.

- A bad hire is the costliest line of all: Gallup puts replacement at 50% to 200% of salary, which means one avoided mis-hire can save more than an entire recruiting campaign, so quality of screening beats volume of sourcing.
- Most salaries are indirect: Pay supports the business broadly, so it sits in indirect costs unless it maps to one traceable task, which matters when you allocate hiring spend accurately.
- Speed and structure cut both sides: Simplifying the workflow trims recruiter hours (indirect) and wasted ad spend (direct) at once, so fix the slowest stage before you spend more on sourcing.
- Evidence-based screening is the highest-impact move: Scoring skills up front with multiple signals prevents the expensive mis-hire, so it pays back across every future cycle, not just the current one.

h3.h3: What counts as a soft cost, and why the headline fee is never the full price

evidence.gloss: Defines indirect hiring costs as the hidden expenses from lost productivity, time, and delays around hiring.
evidence.verbatim:
Indirect hiring costs are the less visible expenses that arise during the hiring process and after a role remains unfilled. They include lost productivity, manager and recruiter time, delayed projects, overtime for existing employees, slower onboarding, and the impact of a poor hire.
Unlike direct costs, these expenses do not appear on an invoice, but they can have a much greater effect on business performance.

evidence.gloss: Explains soft costs as the time/productivity-based expenses that lack a fixed dollar figure but often dominate total spend.
evidence.verbatim:
Soft costs come from the time and productivity invested in making a successful hire. They rarely have a fixed dollar amount, yet they often represent the largest share of hiring costs because they affect multiple teams across the business.
Examples include recruiter and hiring manager time, employee interview hours, productivity lost while a role remains vacant, new hire ramp-up, training, knowledge transfer, and the impact of a poor hire on team performance.

evidence.gloss: Lists concrete examples of indirect hiring costs: lost productivity, recruiter/interviewer time, onboarding, admin overhead, morale, and the cost of a bad hire (Gallup 50-200% of salary).
evidence.verbatim:
Indirect hiring costs are the expenses that never reach an invoice but still hit the bottom line. They come from the time and attention hiring pulls away from the rest of the business, and from the fallout when a hire goes wrong. The big ones:
- Lost productivity: Output dips while a role sits open and again while a new hire ramps, because experienced people split their time to cover and to train.
- Recruiter and interviewer time: The hours HR and your top performers spend reviewing resumes, running interviews, and scoring candidates.
- Onboarding and training: Orientation, tools, and the ramp period before a new hire is fully productive.
- Admin overhead: Payroll setup, benefits enrollment, equipment, and records work for each new person.
- Lower morale: An understaffed, overworked team gets stressed and disengaged, which can trigger more resignations and more vacancies.
- A bad hire: When a hire doesn’t work out, the costs extend far beyond recruiting again. You pay for lost productivity, additional training, separation costs, and the time needed to refill the role. Gallup estimates that replacing an employee costs 50% to 200% of their annual salary.

evidence.gloss: Quoted fee is rarely the full price of filling a role
evidence.verbatim: Whatever fee structure applies to a given role, the quoted number is rarely the full price of filling it.

evidence.gloss: Hidden time/screening costs stack on top of headline fees, scaling with role complexity
evidence.verbatim: These time and screening costs sit on top of, not instead of, the percentage-based or flat agency and search fees described above, and they scale with role complexity in the same direction as the headline fee: senior, specialized, and cleared roles cost more in hidden hours as well as in quoted percentage.

evidence.gloss: Background/reference checks add hidden time cost beyond screening fee
evidence.verbatim: Background and reference checks add further hidden time cost beyond the line-item screening fee: coordinating with previous employers, following up on delayed responses, and — for roles requiring security clearances or specialized certifications — verification that can take weeks and absorb dedicated staff attention throughout[27].

Adding a skills screening step before any interview invite converts a 50-person unscreened pool into an 8-12-person shortlisted pool before any calendar time is consumed. That is where the ROI on assessment spend sits.

evidence.gloss: Table breaking down the main cost drivers (agency fees, interview hours, bad-hire replacement, onboarding waste, early attrition) with the practical lever for each.
evidence.verbatim:
Most organizations have three or four dominant cost drivers; the rest is noise. Job board fees, agency placements, hiring manager interview time, and onboarding waste from wrong-fit hires account for the majority of preventable spend.

 Cost Component What Drives It Practical Reduction Lever 
 Job board/agency fees High applicant volume with low quality signal Add skills screening before sourcing spend; build referral pipeline 
 Interview hours (hiring manager time) Wide unscreened funnel, multiple rounds Screen-first model; one structured interview round replaces three gut-check calls 
 Bad hire replacement Poor competency matching at hire stage Objective test scores before any interview shortlist is built 
 Onboarding waste Wrong-fit hires reach 30+ days before failing Shortlist from assessment results, not resume impressions alone 
 Early attrition (first 90 days) Mismatched expectations or role fit Pre-hire assessments clarify role demands; quality-of-hire metrics catch patterns early 

Agency fees and job board spend are visible and easy to cut. Interview hours and onboarding waste are harder to measure but often larger in aggregate, which is why optimizing only the visible line items misses most of the opportunity.

sections_menu.h2: Referral bonuses vs. agency fees: the per-hire cost gap

h3.h3: The referral bonus itself runs $500-$5,000, averaging about $2,500

evidence.gloss: Employee referral bonus cost range
evidence.verbatim: Employee referral bonuses, a lower-cost channel used mostly for non-executive hiring, commonly land between $500 and $5,000 per successful hire in mid-market companies, and count as external recruiting cost[18].

evidence.gloss: Average referral bonus cited at $2,500
evidence.verbatim: The average employee referral bonus is cited at $2,500[4]

evidence.gloss: Typical referral bonus range $1,000-5,000
evidence.verbatim: with a separate source putting the typical range at $1,000-5,000[3].

h3.h3: A referred hire costs 40-60% less than an agency placement

evidence.gloss: Referred hires cost 40-60% less than agency placements, higher retention
evidence.verbatim: Referred hires cost 40-60% less than agency placements and come with higher retention rates[1].

evidence.gloss: $2,000 referral bonus vs 20% agency fee example
evidence.verbatim: The math is direct: a $2,000 referral bonus beats a 20% agency fee on a $100,000 salary every time[1].

evidence.gloss: Structured referral bonuses ($500-$1,500) undercut agency fees by $9k-$15k per hire; fast payout and simple submission are what keep referral programs working.
evidence.verbatim:
A referral bonus of $500 to $1,500 per successful hire compares to an agency fee of 15-25% of first-year salary. For a $60,000 role, that is a saving of $9,000 to $15,000 per hire versus an agency placement, one of the highest-ROI investments available to any TA budget.

Two things kill referral programs: slow bonus payment and a painful submission process. Pay within 30 days of the new hire’s start date and keep the nomination to a single form.

h3.h3: The other levers: vacancy days, candidate dropout, and bad hires

evidence.gloss: Strategy 8: speed up and humanize the candidate experience to reduce dropout and cost per hire.
evidence.verbatim: Speed and respect win offers. Every extra week in the process raises the odds your top choice takes another job, and it pads that nearly $4,700 average cost per hire. Trim steps, reply quickly, and tell people where they stand. If you need the cost angle, see how to lower your cost per hire without dropping the bar.

evidence.gloss: Explains how services lower cost-per-hire against SHRM's ~$4,700 average by cutting vacancy days and bad hires.
evidence.verbatim: Empty roles are expensive, and so is a slow internal scramble. SHRM puts the cost-per-hire at nearly 4,700 dollars on average. A service can lower that by cutting vacancy days and reducing the bad hires that drive turnover costs.

sections_menu.h2: What the cost-per-hire figure leaves out: vacancy cost, counting errors, and quality

h3.h3: Vacancy cost: roughly $500 a day for an empty role, and time-to-fill is rising

evidence.gloss: Open role is a real, uninvoiced cost with three possible outcomes
evidence.verbatim: A role sitting open is a real, uninvoiced cost: the work either piles up, gets redistributed to already-capacity-constrained teammates, or doesn't get done, and all three outcomes carry a financial consequence[22][20].

evidence.gloss: Vacancy loss estimated at $500/day, $7,000 over two weeks
evidence.verbatim: One figure puts vacancy losses at $500 per day for standard roles, meaning a two-week hiring delay costs $7,000 before an offer is even extended[20].

evidence.gloss: Median time-to-fill rose to 44 days; senior roles 60-90 days
evidence.verbatim: Time-to-fill has been trending longer, which compounds this vacancy cost: median time-to-fill rose to 44 days, up from 31 days in 2023, and senior leadership roles average 60-90 days to fill[20].

evidence.gloss: Time to First Fill: 8 weeks business, 10 weeks technical
evidence.verbatim: A separate benchmarking dataset puts Time to First Fill at 8 weeks for business roles and 10 weeks for technical roles[26].

evidence.gloss: Urgency pushes hiring toward costlier premium channels
evidence.verbatim: Urgency itself becomes a cost multiplier: pressure to fill a role fast pushes teams toward premium channels like agencies and sponsored listings, which carry the steepest per-hire fees, compounding the hard-cost side as well[20].

evidence.gloss: Explains vacancy cost, the productivity loss from an empty role, which SHRM/ANSI excludes, with dollar examples for standard and sales roles and median 2026 time-to-fill of 63.5 days.
evidence.verbatim:
The SHRM/ANSI standard does not include vacancy cost, the productivity loss while a role sits empty:
- Standard role vacancy cost. Typically $500 per day in lost output for an average professional role.
- Revenue-generating role vacancy cost. Sales roles can lose $7,000-$10,000 per month in lost deals.
- Median 2026 time-to-fill. 63.5 days per Employ’s 2026 report, down from 67.7 days in 2025.
- Vacancy cost example. At $500/day x 44 working days = $22,000 in vacancy cost before any recruiting expense.
- Senior sales vacancy. $2,500/day in lost pipeline x 45 days = $112,500 vacancy cost.
- Total loaded cost. True hiring cost combines SHRM/ANSI CPH + vacancy cost + ramp cost + quality risk.

h3.h3: The counting mistakes that distort the number

evidence.gloss: Calculation caveat: time periods must match (annual costs vs annual hires) and hires must be counted as whole, not fractional FTE, or the figure is distorted
evidence.verbatim: Volume comparisons only hold if the time period is matched on both sides of the formula: annual hiring costs should not be measured against monthly or quarterly hire counts, and hires should be counted as whole hires rather than fractional full-time-equivalents, or the resulting per-hire figure is distorted regardless of actual volume[28].

evidence.gloss: Need to segment cost per hire by role/department/type before comparing
evidence.verbatim: Segmenting cost per hire by role level, department, or hiring type before drawing conclusions is necessary because comparing a bulk IC hiring push against a single specialized search on a blended average will misstate both[14].

evidence.gloss: Lists common CPH measurement mistakes (undercounting, ignoring vacancy cost, optimizing cost over quality, inconsistent hire counting, cross-company comparisons) and links to related glossary terms.
evidence.verbatim:
- Undercounting by 30-50%. Per SHRM 2025 benchmarking, organisations using the full ANSI/SHRM methodology reported costs 34% higher than their previously self-reported figures.
- Ignoring vacancy cost. CPH benchmarks compare like-to-like, but the real cost often includes vacancy productivity loss exceeding the recruiting investment.
- Optimising CPH at the expense of quality. Cheapest hires often don’t perform; quality-adjusted CPH is the right metric.
- Including only successful searches. Under SHRM/ANSI, all recruiting costs in a period should be divided by all hires in that period.
- Treating CPH as a stand-alone KPI. Measure alongside time-to-fill, quality-of-hire, candidate experience, and source-of-hire effectiveness.
- Comparing across companies without controls. Industry, role mix, geography, and methodology all affect CPH; apples-to-apples comparisons require careful normalisation.
See also Cost-Benefit Analysis for the broader evaluation framework, Cost Per Impression for upstream recruiting metrics, Churn Rate as a downstream cost amplifier, and Backfill Position for vacancy cost context.

evidence.gloss: Recommends auditing what your ATS/HRIS already calculates automatically (speed metrics) versus what needs manual setup (quality, experience, source).
evidence.verbatim: Before setting any targets, assess what your current ATS, HRIS, and analytics tools are already calculating. Most modern platforms, including Greenhouse, Lever, iCIMS, Workday, and SmartRecruiters, automatically calculate speed metrics. Quality, experience, and source metrics typically require intentional configuration and cross-functional data sharing to be meaningful.

evidence.gloss: Advises collecting two to three months of clean baseline data before setting KPI targets, to avoid pressuring teams to manage numbers instead of improving process.
evidence.verbatim: A minimum of two to three months of clean, consistently collected data is needed before benchmarks are meaningful. Setting aggressive targets against unreliable baselines creates pressure to manage numbers rather than improve processes.

h3.h3: Only 20% track quality of hire alongside cost, and cost alone can be gamed

evidence.gloss: Only 20% of organizations track quality of hire alongside cost-per-hire (SHRM)
evidence.verbatim: Only 20% of organizations track quality of hire alongside cost-per-hire, according to SHRM

evidence.gloss: Defines and explains how to calculate each of the three metrics (cost per hire, quality of hire, time to fill) and why they must be read together.
evidence.verbatim:
Cost per hire equals total recruiting spend divided by total hires in the period. Benchmark internally before comparing to industry figures, which vary too much by sector and seniority to be directly useful.

Quality of hire equals 90-day retention rate plus early performance scores from managers. This is the metric that reveals whether your cost reduction is real or deferred.

Time to fill measures calendar days from role open to offer accepted. Improvements here confirm that your process changes are working end to end, not just reducing spend on one line item while slowing everything else.

Running all three together prevents the most common mistake in TA cost management: optimizing cost per hire in isolation and missing the attrition signal that arrives in the next quarter’s data.

evidence.gloss: A worked numerical example (customer success manager hire) showing ROI at 210% for a good hire versus -45% if that hire leaves at six months.
evidence.verbatim:
Role: a mid-level customer success manager at a $70,000 annual salary. Hard recruiting costs run to $21,000 (30% of salary, per SHRM’s cost-per-hire benchmarks). Soft costs – hiring manager interview time, onboarding coordination, and the first 30 days of reduced productivity – add another $14,000. Total cost to hire: $35,000.

The role sat open for 38 days. SHRM’s 2022 Human Capital Benchmarking Report puts average time to fill at 42 days for professional roles, so 38 days is typical. At $70,000 per year, each unfilled working day costs roughly $269 in lost output (annual salary divided by 260 working days). Vacancy cost: $10,200. Total investment: $45,200.

In year one, the hire retains and expands an account portfolio worth $140,000 in revenue – a conservative two-times salary multiple for a customer success role. Talent acquisition ROI = ($140,000 – $45,200) / $45,200 = 210% . For every dollar spent recruiting this hire, the business returned $3.10.

Now run the bad-hire version. Same $45,200 cost to hire. Hire leaves at month six. Year-one value drops to $70,000 (half the output, half the year). You incur a replacement cost of $45,200 a second time. Total cost: $90,400. Net value: $70,000 – $90,400 = -$20,400. ROI: -45% . One early exit flips a 210% return into a loss. That is the arithmetic case for measuring quality of hire.

evidence.gloss: Notes that cost per hire and time to fill are easy to measure but can be gamed by lowering hiring standards, so they shouldn't be used alone.
evidence.verbatim: Cost per hire and time to fill are the metrics everyone starts with, because they are simple to count. That is also their weakness. They measure effort and speed, not outcome. A recruiter can cut both by lowering the bar, and the numbers will look better right up until the new hire underperforms or quits. Use them, but never alone.

evidence.gloss: Closing summary arguing that reducing total hiring cost requires better hiring decisions, not just lower recruiting spend.
evidence.verbatim:
Direct hiring costs are the numbers everyone sees. Indirect hiring costs are the ones that quietly drain far more money through lost productivity, vacant roles, and poor hiring decisions. If you only measure invoices, you only measure part of the problem.
The most effective way to reduce total hiring cost is not simply spending less on recruiting. It is making better hiring decisions from the start. A structured, skills-first hiring process helps you identify qualified candidates faster, avoid costly mis-hires, and improve long-term retention, delivering a stronger return on every hire you make.
